summary_html: Reports via **state hotlines** (anonymous or confidential). CAPTA conditions funding on operating intake systems with confidentiality and good-faith protections. Wyoming operates no statewide child abuse hotline — Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-206(b) says the state agency "may" establish one — so reports go to the county DFS field office, or to 911 and law enforcement in an emergency.
authority_html: - **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — intake, confidentiality, immunity, and data requirements tied to federal funding

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court held that Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-205(a) obliges any person with reasonable cause to suspect abuse to report immediately, and that a reporter who meets that threshold acts in good faith and is immune under § 14-3-209, as are those who later participate in the investigation.
key_cases.relevance: Anonymous or hotline reporters are shielded by the presumption of good faith, which negligence alone cannot overcome.
key_cases.quote: the plain language of § 14-3-205(a) does not require that the reporting party know that a child has been abused, or even reasonably believe that the child was abused

key_cases.holding: The Court held Wyoming's child-abuse reporting statute confers qualified, not absolute, immunity: a reporter who reports in good faith is immune, good faith is presumed, and mere negligence in reporting does not defeat the presumption.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Wyoming statement of the reporter-immunity rule that governs who may be held liable for a child-abuse report at this decision point, and of the presumption of good faith a plaintiff must overcome.
key_cases.quote: the Wyoming legislature intended to provide qualified immunity, that is immunity for all who report child abuse in good faith

key_cases.case_name: May v. Southeast Wyoming Mental Health Center
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment for the reporting therapist and the investigating public employees, holding that § 14-3-209 immunity is not confined to the act of reporting but covers participation in the investigation, and that the Governmental Claims Act separately immunized the state actors.
key_cases.relevance: Supports the confidentiality-and-immunity architecture behind Wyoming's hotline intake.
key_cases.quote: Section 14-3-209 does not limit immunity to suits based only on the reporting

state_agency.name: Wyoming Department of Family Services
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the DFS field office in the county where the child lives — the list is at dfs.wyo.gov/about/contact-us

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(a)

Staff of a medical or other public or private institution, school, facility or agency must also notify the person in charge, who is then also responsible for making the report — Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(b)

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Notification of a suspected case of child abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in statute; Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-204(a)(iii) states the duty without a penalty, and the agency must seek a court order if denied reasonable access to the child

parent_rights_at_moment: Right to refuse entry without warrant
Right to be advised of the specific complaints or allegations against you at the initial time of contact (Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-204(a)(iii))
A DFS caseworker cannot take your child: only a law enforcement officer, a treating physician, physician's assistant or nurse practitioner, or a court order can (Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-405)
what_to_say: I do not consent to entry without a warrant
Please provide your card and the allegations in writing
I will have my attorney contact you
what_not_to_do: Do not let them in 'just to look'
